unit.title: Revolution: Ideas & Voices Study Tool
unit.subtitle: What made independence worth fighting for? Learn the vocabulary, follow the road to revolution, and build your podcast research skills.
unit.essentialQuestion: What made independence worth fighting for — and for whom was it left incomplete?

vocabulary.definition: A British order banning colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains after the French and Indian War
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Britain won a huge war and then told colonists: that western land you fought for? Off limits. It was meant to keep peace with Native nations, but to colonists it felt like a locked door — the first crack between Britain and its colonies.
vocabulary.example: A Virginia farmer hoping to claim land in the Ohio Valley found the Proclamation of 1763 had slammed the door shut
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Proclamation of 1763 banned colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains. Britain hoped to prevent conflict with Native nations after the French and Indian War. Colonists who wanted that land saw the proclamation as the first sign that Britain would put its own interests ahead of theirs.

vocabulary.definition: Being taxed by a government in which you have no elected voice
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Imagine the ASB charging you fees when you're not allowed to vote for ASB officers. Colonists paid taxes passed by a Parliament an ocean away, where not a single seat belonged to them — and that, more than the money itself, is what made them furious.
vocabulary.example: The Stamp Act taxed newspapers and legal papers, and colonists protested that no one in Parliament represented them
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Taxation without representation means being taxed by a government in which you have no elected voice. Colonists paid taxes passed by a Parliament where they held no seats at all. Their rallying cry was less about the money and more about the principle of having a say.

vocabulary.definition: An organized refusal to buy certain goods as a form of protest
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Protest with your wallet. When colonists stopped buying British tea, cloth, and paper, British merchants lost money fast — and suddenly Parliament started listening. It was one of the few weapons every colonist, including women running households, could use.
vocabulary.example: Colonial women organized boycotts of British cloth, spinning their own homespun fabric instead
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A boycott is an organized refusal to buy certain goods as a form of protest. Colonists boycotted British products to pressure Parliament into repealing unpopular taxes. Because everyone shops, boycotts let ordinary people, including women and children, take part in the resistance.

vocabulary.definition: To officially cancel a law
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: When protests and boycotts worked, Parliament would repeal — officially cancel — a hated tax. The Stamp Act lasted barely a year before it was repealed. Each repeal taught colonists a dangerous lesson: pressure works.
vocabulary.example: After months of colonial boycotts, Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766
vocabulary.typingSnippet: To repeal a law is to officially cancel it. Parliament repealed the Stamp Act after colonial boycotts hurt British merchants. Every repeal proved to colonists that organized resistance could actually change what a government did.

vocabulary.definition: The 1774 laws punishing Massachusetts for the Boston Tea Party, which Britain called the Coercive Acts
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Britain's punishment for the Boston Tea Party: close Boston Harbor until the tea was paid for, shut down Massachusetts self-government, and force colonists to house British soldiers in their towns (quartering). Meant to isolate Boston, the acts backfired — the other colonies rushed to help.
vocabulary.example: When the Intolerable Acts closed Boston Harbor, other colonies sent food and supplies overland to the city
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Intolerable Acts were the 1774 laws that punished Massachusetts for the Boston Tea Party. They closed Boston Harbor, shut down local government, and forced colonists to quarter British troops. Instead of isolating Boston, the acts united the colonies against Britain.

vocabulary.definition: A colonist who supported independence from Britain
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The side that said: enough — we should govern ourselves. Patriots ranged from firebrands like Samuel Adams to farmers who had never left their county. Choosing this side meant risking your property, and if the Revolution failed, your life.
vocabulary.example: Mercy Otis Warren used her pen as a Patriot, writing plays that mocked British officials
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A Patriot was a colonist who supported independence from Britain. Patriots came from every colony and every walk of life, from wealthy lawyers to poor farmers. Declaring yourself a Patriot was a serious risk, because if the Revolution failed it would be treason.

vocabulary.definition: A colonist who stayed loyal to Britain and the king during the Revolution
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Roughly one in five white colonists picked the other side — and they had reasons. Some believed Britain protected them, some depended on British trade, and many enslaved people saw more promise of freedom in British lines than in Patriot ones. History is more complicated than heroes and villains.
vocabulary.example: Thousands of Loyalists fled to Canada after the war, losing their homes and property
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A Loyalist was a colonist who stayed loyal to Britain and the king. Loyalists had many motives, from business ties to a genuine belief that British rule was best. Understanding their perspective is essential to telling the full story of the Revolution.

vocabulary.definition: Choosing not to take either side in a conflict
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Not everyone picked a team. Many colonists — Quakers whose faith forbade war, families just trying to survive, communities caught between armies — stayed neutral. But when the war arrived at your doorstep, neutrality got harder and harder to keep.
vocabulary.example: Many Quakers in Pennsylvania stayed neutral because their religious beliefs opposed all war
vocabulary.typingSnippet: To be neutral is to take neither side in a conflict. Many colonists tried to stay neutral during the Revolution, whether from religious belief or self-preservation. As the war spread, staying out of it became nearly impossible.

vocabulary.definition: Open, organized resistance against a government or authority
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: When protest stops asking and starts defying. To Britain, the colonists were rebels breaking the law; to Patriots, rebellion was the last option left after every petition was ignored. Whether a rebellion becomes a 'revolution' usually depends on who wins — and who writes the story.
vocabulary.example: King George declared the colonies in open rebellion in 1775, months before the Declaration of Independence
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A rebellion is open, organized resistance against a government or authority. Britain saw the colonists as rebels, while Patriots saw themselves as defenders of their rights. The same events can look like crime or courage depending on whose perspective you take.

vocabulary.definition: Colonial militia members trained to be ready to fight at a minute's notice
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Think of a volunteer fire crew: ordinary townspeople, farmers, blacksmiths and shopkeepers, who kept their muskets by the door and promised to turn out fast when the alarm came. At Lexington in April 1775, minutemen were the first to face British soldiers.
vocabulary.example: When riders spread the alarm on the night of April 18, 1775, minutemen gathered on Lexington Green before dawn
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Minutemen were colonial militia members trained to be ready to fight at a minute's notice. They were farmers and craftsmen, not full-time soldiers. On April 19, 1775, minutemen faced British troops at Lexington and Concord, and the Revolutionary War began.

vocabulary.definition: When a conflict grows step by step, each side's response making the next fight bigger
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Picture an argument where every reply is a little louder than the last, until it turns into a shoving match. From 1763 to 1775, each British law and each colonial protest pushed the other side to go further.
vocabulary.example: The Boston Tea Party led to the Intolerable Acts, which led colonies to unite, which led to fighting at Lexington: escalation
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Escalation is when a conflict grows step by step, each side's response making the next fight bigger. After 1763, every new British law brought a bigger protest, and every protest brought a harsher law, until the colonies and Britain were at war.

vocabulary.definition: Freedom from control by another country; the right of a people to govern themselves
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The big prize: no more king, no more Parliament — Americans making American laws. Declaring it in 1776 was the easy part; winning it took seven more years of war, and deciding who actually got to enjoy it took far longer.
vocabulary.example: The colonies declared independence in July 1776, but Britain did not recognize it until the Treaty of Paris in 1783
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Independence is freedom from control by another country and the right of a people to govern themselves. The colonies declared independence in 1776 and fought seven more years to win it. Our driving question asks what made it worth fighting for, and for whom it was left incomplete.

vocabulary.definition: Rights that belong to every person and cannot be taken away or given up, such as life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Rights you're born with — not gifts from a king that can be revoked. The Declaration names three: life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. The bold claim was that these belong to everyone; the painful truth was that the new nation denied them to millions.
vocabulary.example: Jefferson wrote that all people are endowed with unalienable rights, even as he enslaved more than 600 people in his lifetime
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Unalienable rights are rights that belong to every person and cannot be taken away or given up. The Declaration of Independence names life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. Generations of Americans have fought to make that promise apply to everyone.

vocabulary.definition: The idea that a government's power comes from the agreement of the people it rules
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Governments work for the people, not the other way around. If rulers only have power because the people agree to it, then the people can withdraw that agreement — which is exactly the argument the Declaration makes for breaking up with Britain.
vocabulary.example: The Declaration argues that because Britain ruled the colonies without their consent, the colonists had the right to form their own government
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Consent of the governed is the idea that a government's power comes from the agreement of the people it rules. The Declaration used this idea to justify breaking away from Britain. It remains the core principle behind voting and representative government today.

vocabulary.definition: The cruel and unjust use of power by a ruler or government
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Power with no limits and no accountability. The Declaration is basically a breakup letter with a list of receipts — 27 grievances accusing King George of tyranny, from dissolving colonial legislatures to keeping standing armies in peacetime.
vocabulary.example: The Declaration lists 27 grievances to prove the king's 'absolute tyranny over these States'
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Tyranny is the cruel and unjust use of power by a ruler or government. The Declaration of Independence accuses King George of tyranny and lists dozens of specific grievances as evidence. Fear of tyranny later shaped how Americans designed their Constitution.

vocabulary.definition: A complaint about something believed to be wrong or unfair
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: It's more than a gripe. A grievance is a complaint you can point to and explain. The Declaration of Independence is mostly a list of them, each one meant to prove the king had treated the colonies unfairly.
vocabulary.example: One grievance in the Declaration accuses the king of "imposing Taxes on us without our Consent"
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A grievance is a complaint about something believed to be wrong or unfair. Most of the Declaration of Independence is a list of 27 grievances against King George III, from taxing colonists without their consent to taking away trial by jury.

vocabulary.definition: The crime of betraying your own country or ruler, especially by fighting against it
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: To Britain, the colonists were British subjects, so declaring independence was not a brave new start. It was treason, and the punishment for treason was death. The signers knew they were risking their lives.
vocabulary.example: If Britain had won the war, the signers of the Declaration could have been hanged for treason
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Treason is the crime of betraying your own country or ruler, especially by fighting against it. When the colonists declared independence, Britain saw it as treason. The men who signed the Declaration knew they could be hanged if the war was lost.

vocabulary.definition: A clear, arguable claim that your evidence works to prove
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The backbone of your podcast episode. Not a fact ('Deborah Sampson was a soldier') and not a topic ('my episode is about spies') — a claim someone could push back on, that every source you cite helps you defend.
vocabulary.example: A strong thesis: 'James Armistead Lafayette’s spying helped trap the British at Yorktown, yet the nation he helped free made him petition for his own freedom'
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A thesis is a clear, arguable claim that your evidence works to prove. It is not a fact or a topic, but a position someone could disagree with. Every source in your podcast episode should help defend your thesis.

vocabulary.definition: How trustworthy and reliable a source of information is
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Before you trust a source, interrogate it: Who made this? When? Why? What do they gain if you believe them? A museum's research page and a random meme might make the same claim — but they haven't earned the same trust.
vocabulary.example: For your podcast, a Library of Congress page about Phillis Wheatley has more credibility than an unsourced fan site
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Credibility is how trustworthy and reliable a source of information is. Historians judge credibility by asking who created a source, when, and for what purpose. Building your podcast on credible sources is what separates research from rumor.

vocabulary.definition: A note giving credit to the source your information came from
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Your receipts. A citation tells your audience exactly where each fact came from, so they can check it themselves. It gives credit to the people who did the work — and it's what makes your podcast trustworthy instead of just confident.
vocabulary.example: Your podcast script ends with citations for every source you used, from primary documents to museum websites
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A citation is a note giving credit to the source your information came from. Citations let your audience verify your facts and give credit to the researchers who found them. In this project, every claim in your script needs a citation to back it up.

vocabulary.definition: People whose real roles in history rarely make it into the usual telling of the story
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The Revolution was won by more than the faces on money. Poets like Phillis Wheatley, spies like James Armistead Lafayette, soldiers like Deborah Sampson, leaders like Joseph Brant, and thinkers like Abigail Adams and Mercy Otis Warren all shaped it — your podcast puts one of them back in the story.
vocabulary.example: Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Native descent, was the first to die at the Boston Massacre — yet many textbooks give him a single sentence
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Overlooked voices are people whose real roles in history rarely make it into the usual telling. Women, African Americans, and Native nations all shaped the Revolution, yet their stories are often reduced to a sentence or skipped entirely. Recovering those voices is the whole point of our podcast project.

vocabulary.definition: A record created by someone who was there at the time, such as a letter, diary, newspaper, or picture
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: It's evidence straight from the time. George Washington's 1767 letter about the Proclamation is a primary source because he wrote it while it was happening.
vocabulary.example: A witness's testimony at the 1770 Boston Massacre trial is a primary source
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A primary source is a record created by someone who was there at the time, such as a letter, diary, newspaper, or picture. Primary sources show what people thought and saw in their own moment, but they also show that person's point of view.

vocabulary.definition: An account written later by someone who studied the past but was not there, such as a textbook or history book
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: A secondary source is someone else explaining history after studying it, like your textbook or a museum website. It can give the big picture, but it is one step away from the events.
vocabulary.example: A 2004 biography of Deborah Sampson, written by a historian who studied her records, is a secondary source
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A secondary source is an account written later by someone who studied the past but was not there, such as a textbook or history book. Secondary sources explain the big picture, and good ones show which primary sources they used.

timelineEvents.title: Treaty of Paris ends the French & Indian War
timelineEvents.description: France gives Canada and its land east of the Mississippi to Britain. Britain has won, but its war debt has nearly doubled.

timelineEvents.title: Proclamation of 1763
timelineEvents.description: Britain bans settlement west of the Appalachians, angering colonists who expected that land

timelineEvents.title: Stamp Act
timelineEvents.description: The first direct tax on the colonies sparks the cry of taxation without representation

timelineEvents.title: Townshend Acts
timelineEvents.description: New taxes on glass, paint, lead, paper and tea bring a second boycott. In 1770 Parliament repeals all of the new taxes except the tax on tea

timelineEvents.title: Boston Massacre
timelineEvents.description: British soldiers fire into a crowd, killing five colonists including Crispus Attucks

timelineEvents.title: Boston Tea Party
timelineEvents.description: Colonists dump 342 chests of British tea into Boston Harbor to protest the Tea Act

timelineEvents.title: Intolerable Acts
timelineEvents.description: Britain punishes Massachusetts by closing Boston Harbor and quartering troops, uniting the colonies instead

timelineEvents.title: First Continental Congress
timelineEvents.description: Delegates from twelve colonies meet in Philadelphia to coordinate a response to Britain

timelineEvents.title: Battles of Lexington & Concord
timelineEvents.description: The 'shot heard round the world': the Revolutionary War begins in Massachusetts

timelineEvents.title: Declaration of Independence
timelineEvents.description: Congress declares the colonies free and independent states, justified by unalienable rights and consent of the governed

timelineEvents.title: Treaty of Paris
timelineEvents.description: Britain officially recognizes American independence, ending the Revolutionary War

practiceQuestions.question: Why did Britain and France go to war in North America in 1754?
options: They both wanted to rule over England itself
They both claimed the land of the Ohio River Valley
France wanted to end the Atlantic slave trade
Britain wanted to stop colonists from moving east
practiceQuestions.explanation: Both empires claimed the Ohio Valley. French forts and British colonists moving west collided there in 1754.

practiceQuestions.question: What did France lose in the Treaty of Paris of 1763?
options: Canada and almost all of its land in North America
Only its sugar islands in the West Indies and Africa
Florida, which it then gave to the thirteen colonies
Nothing at all, because the war ended in a tie
practiceQuestions.explanation: France gave Canada and its land east of the Mississippi to Britain. (It had already handed Louisiana to Spain in a separate deal.)

practiceQuestions.question: Why did Britain look to the colonies for money after the French & Indian War?
options: The colonies had lost the war and owed Britain
The king wanted to build a new palace in Boston
Britain's war debt had nearly doubled
The colonies asked Parliament to raise their taxes
practiceQuestions.explanation: Britain won, but borrowing to pay for the war nearly doubled its debt. Parliament decided the colonies should help pay.

practiceQuestions.question: Why did the Proclamation of 1763 anger colonists?
options: It placed a new tax on tea and paper goods
It made colonists house British soldiers
It closed Boston Harbor to all trade ships
It banned settling west of the Appalachians
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Proclamation closed the land west of the Appalachians to colonial settlement, land many colonists had expected to claim after the war.

practiceQuestions.question: In his 1767 letter to William Crawford, how did George Washington describe the Proclamation?
options: As a quick fix that would end in a few years
As a fair law that colonists should obey
As a reason to declare independence right away
As a gift to colonists from the king
practiceQuestions.explanation: Washington called it "a temporary expedient to quiet the Minds of the Indians" and planned to claim western land anyway, in secret.

practiceQuestions.question: What did the Quartering Act require colonists to do?
options: Pay a tax on every newspaper and legal paper
House and supply British soldiers
Stop trading with any country but Britain
Move east of the Appalachian Mountains
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Quartering Act of 1765 made colonies provide housing and supplies for British troops.

practiceQuestions.question: What did colonists mean by "no taxation without representation"?
options: No one in the colonies should ever pay a tax
Only British citizens living in England should pay taxes
Only their own elected representatives should tax them
Taxes should be paid in goods, not in money
practiceQuestions.explanation: Colonists elected no one to Parliament, so they argued Parliament had no right to tax them.

practiceQuestions.question: What did the Stamp Act of 1765 tax?
options: Printed papers like newspapers and legal documents
Imported goods like tea, glass, paint and lead
Land that colonists owned west of the mountains
Clothing, shoes and other household goods
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Stamp Act taxed printed paper: newspapers, legal documents, even playing cards.

practiceQuestions.question: How did colonists get the Stamp Act repealed in 1766?
options: They won a battle against British soldiers in Boston
They elected their own members to sit in Parliament
They asked the king to dismiss Parliament for a year
They boycotted British goods until merchants lost money
practiceQuestions.explanation: Colonists stopped buying British goods. British merchants lost money and pushed Parliament to repeal the tax.

practiceQuestions.question: What is a boycott?
options: An organized refusal to buy certain goods
A law that cancels an earlier law
A tax on goods brought in from another place
A meeting of leaders from different colonies
practiceQuestions.explanation: A boycott is a protest with your wallet: people agree together not to buy something.

practiceQuestions.question: What did the Townshend Acts of 1767 tax?
options: Newspapers, legal papers and playing cards
Land that colonists owned west of the mountains
Every ship that sailed out of a colonial port
Imported goods like glass, paint, paper and tea
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Townshend Acts taxed goods the colonies imported from Britain. Colonists boycotted them, and Parliament dropped every tax but the one on tea in 1770.

practiceQuestions.question: In 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston and killed five people, including Crispus Attucks. What is this event called?
options: The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Massacre
The Battle of Lexington
The Intolerable Acts
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Boston Massacre, March 5, 1770. Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Native descent, was among those killed.

practiceQuestions.question: What were colonists protesting at the Boston Tea Party in 1773?
options: The Quartering Act and the soldiers living in Boston
The Proclamation Line along the Appalachian Mountains
Parliament's tax on tea and its rules for selling it
The arrest of leaders of the First Continental Congress
practiceQuestions.explanation: Colonists dumped British tea into Boston Harbor to protest Parliament's tea tax and the Tea Act of 1773.

practiceQuestions.question: What were the Intolerable Acts a response to?
options: The Boston Tea Party
The Stamp Act protests
The Battle of Lexington
The Declaration of Independence
practiceQuestions.explanation: Parliament passed them in 1774 to punish Massachusetts for the Boston Tea Party. Britain called them the Coercive Acts.

practiceQuestions.question: What did the Intolerable Acts do to the other colonies?
options: They made the other colonies turn against Boston
They had no effect outside Massachusetts
They made the other colonies stop all trade with Boston
They pulled the colonies together to help Boston
practiceQuestions.explanation: Britain meant to isolate Boston. Instead, other colonies sent food and supplies and met at the First Continental Congress.

practiceQuestions.question: Why did the First Continental Congress meet in Philadelphia in 1774?
options: To plan a joint response to Britain, including a boycott
To sign the Declaration of Independence from Britain
To elect George Washington as the first president
To write the Articles of Confederation for the states
practiceQuestions.explanation: Delegates from twelve colonies agreed to boycott British goods and to meet again if things did not change.

practiceQuestions.question: Why do the Battles of Lexington and Concord (1775) matter?
options: They were the last battles of the Revolutionary War
They were the first fighting of the Revolutionary War
They were where the Declaration of Independence was signed
They finally forced Parliament to repeal the Stamp Act
practiceQuestions.explanation: On April 19, 1775, British soldiers and colonial militia fought at Lexington and Concord: the first battles of the war.

practiceQuestions.question: What was a Patriot during the Revolution?
options: A colonist who stayed loyal to King George III of Britain
A colonist who refused to take either side in the war
A colonist who supported independence from Britain
A British soldier who fought in the colonies
practiceQuestions.explanation: Patriots supported independence. About one in five white colonists stayed loyal to the king instead.

practiceQuestions.question: What was a Loyalist (also called a Tory)?
options: A colonist who supported independence from Britain
A colonist who fought alongside Native nations
A spy who secretly worked for both sides at once
A colonist who stayed loyal to the British king
practiceQuestions.explanation: Loyalists stayed loyal to the Crown, for reasons like business ties, government jobs, family or fear of war.

practiceQuestions.question: What did it mean to stay neutral in the Revolution?
options: To fight for whichever side paid more
To support the Patriots without fighting
To not take either side
To move to Britain until the war ended
practiceQuestions.explanation: Many colonists tried to stay out of the fight and protect their families and farms.

practiceQuestions.question: Why did some enslaved people side with the British?
options: A British governor promised freedom to those who joined the British
The British promised each of them free land in the Ohio Valley
Patriot leaders ordered them to go and join the British army
The British paid them twice as much as the Patriot army offered
practiceQuestions.explanation: In 1775, Lord Dunmore, the royal governor of Virginia, promised freedom to enslaved people who escaped Patriot enslavers and joined British forces.

practiceQuestions.question: Why did different people take different sides on independence?
options: Everyone in a colony thought the same way about the king
Their background and circumstances shaped what they wanted
Only wealthy colonists were allowed to have opinions on it
The king told each colony which side it had to take
practiceQuestions.explanation: Where you lived, what you did for work, your family and whether you were free all shaped your view of independence.

practiceQuestions.question: What turns a protest into a rebellion?
options: When people ask the government politely to change a law
When people agree together to stop buying certain goods
When people write a letter to the king about a problem
When people openly defy the government and its power
practiceQuestions.explanation: A protest asks for change. A rebellion is open, organized resistance against the government itself.

practiceQuestions.question: What does "unalienable rights" mean in the Declaration of Independence?
options: Rights that cannot be taken away
Rights the government gives out each year
Rights that belong only to landowners
Rights that must be earned by serving
practiceQuestions.explanation: Unalienable rights belong to every person from birth. No king can grant them or take them away.

practiceQuestions.question: Which three rights does the Declaration name?
options: Freedom, justice, equality and safety for all
Liberty, property, security and fair trials
Life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness
Speech, religion and the right to vote freely
practiceQuestions.explanation: "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness."

practiceQuestions.question: What does "consent of the governed" mean?
options: The king decides who may vote
Only rich people should be allowed to vote
Government gets its power from the people
Kings get their power to rule from God
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Declaration argues a government only has the power the people agree to give it.

practiceQuestions.question: According to the Declaration, what can people do when a government destroys their rights?
options: Change or get rid of that government
Accept it, because rebellion is always wrong
Move to a different country
Wait for the king to fix it
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Declaration says people have the right "to alter or to abolish" a government that destroys their rights.

practiceQuestions.question: What did the Declaration accuse King George III of?
options: Being too generous with the colonies
Starting the French & Indian War
Not paying enough attention to the colonies
Repeated injuries meant to create a tyranny
practiceQuestions.explanation: The long list of grievances charges the king with "repeated injuries and usurpations," all aimed at "an absolute Tyranny."

practiceQuestions.question: The colonists asked Britain for change many times before declaring independence. What does this show?
options: The colonists were too afraid to fight Britain
Independence came after peaceful attempts failed
King George was always willing to compromise
The colonists never really wanted independence at all
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Declaration says the colonists "Petitioned for Redress" again and again and were answered "only by repeated injury."

practiceQuestions.question: When Jefferson wrote "all men are created equal," whose rights were left out?
options: Members of the Continental Congress
Loyalists who had left for Canada
British soldiers serving in the colonies
Women, enslaved people and Native nations
practiceQuestions.explanation: Women almost everywhere could not vote, enslaved people had no liberty at all, and the Declaration itself calls Native people "merciless Indian Savages."

practiceQuestions.question: Which of these is a thesis?
options: Phillis Wheatley was born in West Africa in about 1753 and enslaved in Boston
Phillis Wheatley's poems proved the colonists wrong about who could be a writer
This podcast episode is all about the life and poems of Phillis Wheatley
Phillis Wheatley wrote poems and published a book of them in London in 1773
practiceQuestions.explanation: A thesis is an arguable claim your evidence works to prove. The others are a fact, a topic and a fact.

practiceQuestions.question: Which question best checks a source's credibility?
options: How long is the source?
Does the source agree with what I already think?
Who made this source, when, and why?
Does the source have pictures?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Who made it, when and why tells you whether a source has earned your trust.

practiceQuestions.question: Why does a podcast script need citations?
options: To give credit to the sources the facts came from
To make the script longer so it meets the time
To show the listener which parts are made up
To replace the need for a thesis in the intro
practiceQuestions.explanation: A citation is your receipt: it shows where every fact came from so a listener can check it.

practiceQuestions.question: Who led Native nations in attacks on British forts around the Great Lakes in 1763?
options: George Washington, a Virginia militia officer
Pontiac, an Ottawa leader
William Pitt, a British war leader
Joseph Brant, a Mohawk leader
practiceQuestions.explanation: Pontiac's War began in 1763. Britain answered with the Proclamation of 1763 to avoid another costly frontier war.

practiceQuestions.question: On the same day Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766, what did it pass?
options: A law giving each colony two elected seats in the House of Commons
A law ending the tax on tea for good so that the boycotts would stop
The Declaratory Act, saying it could make colony laws "in all cases whatsoever"
A law closing Boston Harbor until every unused stamp was paid for in full
practiceQuestions.explanation: Repeal was not surrender: the Declaratory Act said Parliament still had full power over the colonies.

practiceQuestions.question: Why did most Native nations side with Britain during the Revolution?
options: Britain had tried to limit colonial settlement on their land
Britain promised them seats in Parliament
The colonists refused to trade with them at all
France ordered its old allies to fight for Britain
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Proclamation Line had tried to keep settlers out. Native leaders judged that a colonial victory would cost them their homelands.

practiceQuestions.question: What did Lord Dunmore, the royal governor of Virginia, promise in November 1775?
options: Free land in Canada to every Loyalist family who left the colonies
A lower tax on tea for any colonist who stayed loyal to the king
A year of pay to any Patriot soldier who switched to the British side
Freedom to enslaved people who escaped Patriot enslavers and fought for Britain
practiceQuestions.explanation: Dunmore's Proclamation led thousands of enslaved people to risk escape to British lines.

practiceQuestions.question: Who were the minutemen?
options: British soldiers housed in colonists' homes
Colonial militia ready to fight at a minute's notice
Messengers who carried letters to the king
Loyalists who spied for the British army
practiceQuestions.explanation: Minutemen were ordinary farmers and craftsmen. They faced British troops at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775.

practiceQuestions.question: What does escalation mean on the road to revolution?
options: Each side's response made the next conflict bigger
Colonists moved west across the mountains
Britain slowly lowered its taxes over time
The colonies voted on each new law together
practiceQuestions.explanation: Taxes led to boycotts, troops led to the Boston Massacre, the Tea Party led to the Intolerable Acts, and those led to war.

practiceQuestions.question: Why does the Olive Branch Petition (July 1775) matter?
options: It was the first tax the colonists agreed to pay without a boycott
It ended the fighting at Lexington and Concord with a peace treaty
It was Congress's last peaceful offer, and the king refused to read it
It gave each colony one elected seat in Parliament for the first time
practiceQuestions.explanation: George III refused it and in August declared the colonies in open rebellion, which pushed many colonists toward independence.

practiceQuestions.question: What did Thomas Paine argue in Common Sense (January 1776)?
options: The colonies should pay Britain's war debt quickly
Colonists should stay neutral in the war
Parliament should give the colonies more seats
The colonies should break away from Britain completely
practiceQuestions.explanation: Paine wrote in plain language that it was absurd for an island to rule a continent. The pamphlet moved many undecided colonists.

practiceQuestions.question: Why can no king take away unalienable rights, according to the Declaration?
options: Parliament voted to protect them forever in the Stamp Act of 1765
People are born with them; they are not gifts from a ruler
They are written into every colonial charter the king ever signed
Only the elected colonial assemblies are allowed to change them
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rights you are born with do not come from a king, so a king has no power to take them back.

practiceQuestions.question: According to the Declaration, where does a government get its power?
options: From the agreement of the people it rules
From the king, who receives it from God
From the army that protects the country
From the richest landowners in each colony
practiceQuestions.explanation: This is consent of the governed: "deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed."

practiceQuestions.question: Which thinker's idea of natural rights to life, liberty and property shaped the Declaration?
options: Thomas Paine
King George III
John Locke
William Pitt
practiceQuestions.explanation: Locke wrote in 1689 that people are born with natural rights and may resist rulers who violate them.

practiceQuestions.question: What is a grievance?
options: A law passed by Parliament for the colonies without a vote
A promise to fight for independence until the war is won
A tax on paper goods like newspapers and playing cards
A complaint about something believed to be wrong or unfair
practiceQuestions.explanation: Most of the Declaration is a list of 27 grievances against King George III.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of these is a grievance the Declaration lists against the king?
options: "For imposing Taxes on us without our Consent"
"For refusing to sell tea to the colonies"
"For moving the capital away from Boston"
"For forbidding colonists to build any ships"
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Declaration names taxing without consent as one example of the king's tyranny.

practiceQuestions.question: Why was signing the Declaration so dangerous for the signers?
options: They would lose the seats they held in Parliament in London
France had threatened to arrest them if they sided with Spain
Britain saw it as treason, which was punished by death
Their colonies would have to pay new taxes on every signed paper
practiceQuestions.explanation: To Britain, declaring independence was treason. The signers were betting their lives on winning the war.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of these is a primary source about the Boston Massacre?
options: A witness's testimony at the soldiers' trial in 1770
A textbook chapter about the event written in 2015
A museum website article about the event
A documentary about the event made in 2020
practiceQuestions.explanation: The witness was there and spoke at the time, so the testimony is a primary source.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of these is a secondary source?
options: Abigail Adams's 1776 letter to John Adams
A historian's 2004 book about Deborah Sampson
A newspaper printed in Boston in 1773
George Washington's 1767 letter to Crawford
practiceQuestions.explanation: A secondary source is written later by someone who studied the past but was not there.

practiceQuestions.question: Who are "overlooked voices" in the history of the Revolution?
options: Only the 56 men who signed the Declaration of Independence in 1776
British leaders in Parliament who made the laws for the colonies
People whose real roles rarely make it into the usual telling of the story
Colonists who never left their own towns during the whole war
practiceQuestions.explanation: Women, Black Americans, Native people and poor colonists shaped the Revolution but are often left out of the story.

practiceQuestions.question: Why is James Armistead Lafayette an overlooked voice?
options: He signed the Declaration of Independence, but his name was later erased
He led the British army at Yorktown and then joined the Patriots
He wrote Common Sense under a different name to keep himself safe
His spying helped win Yorktown, yet he had to petition for his own freedom
practiceQuestions.explanation: Armistead, enslaved in Virginia, spied on the British in 1781. Virginia did not free him until he petitioned years later.

practiceQuestions.question: What should a citation for a podcast source include?
options: The author, the title, the publisher or website, and the date
Only the website address, copied from the top of the page
Your own opinion of whether the source's topic is interesting
The number of people who have read or shared the source online
practiceQuestions.explanation: A citation tells listeners exactly where a fact came from so they can check it.

practiceQuestions.question: Two websites disagree about what Molly Pitcher did. What should a careful researcher do?
options: Use whichever site has more pictures
Pick the site that agrees with your thesis
Leave the person out of the episode
Check what other credible sources agree on
practiceQuestions.explanation: Corroborating, checking a claim against other credible sources, is how historians separate documented history from legend.

shortAnswerQuestions.question: Which event pushed the colonists closest to rebellion, and what made it worse than the events before it?
shortAnswerQuestions.rubric: Strong response names one specific event, explains with details what it did to colonists, and compares it with earlier events to show what made it a tipping point (for example, punishing a whole colony rather than taxing goods).
shortAnswerQuestions.exemplar: The Intolerable Acts pushed the colonists closest to rebellion. Earlier laws like the Stamp Act taxed goods, and colonists could fight back with boycotts until Parliament repealed them. The Intolerable Acts were different: they punished everyone in Massachusetts for the Boston Tea Party. Britain closed Boston Harbor, so people could not work or get supplies, and it took away Massachusetts' right to govern itself. This showed colonists that Britain would destroy a whole colony's freedom to make a point, so the other colonies started working together against Britain.

plan.text: The Intolerable Acts pushed the colonists closest to rebellion, because they punished a whole colony instead of just taxing goods.
Britain closed Boston Harbor in 1774, so people in Boston could not work or get supplies.
Britain also took away Massachusetts' right to govern itself.
Earlier taxes could be beaten with boycotts, but this showed Britain would take away colonists' freedom, so other colonies joined Massachusetts against Britain.

sentenceStarters: The event that pushed colonists closest to rebellion was ___ because ___.
shortAnswerQuestions.lookAt: the timeline, and Chapter 1, Section 3 of the reading (Boston and the Intolerable Acts).

shortAnswerQuestions.question: What changed between 1763 and 1775 that turned colonists' protests into fighting?
shortAnswerQuestions.rubric: Strong response explains escalation: names at least two events in order, shows how each response made the next conflict worse, and explains why peaceful protest no longer seemed to work by 1775.
shortAnswerQuestions.exemplar: Over those twelve years, colonists tried peaceful ways to change Britain's rules, and each time Britain answered with something harsher. Boycotts got the Stamp Act repealed, but Parliament passed new taxes in the Townshend Acts. When colonists protested, Britain sent troops to Boston, and soldiers killed five people in the Boston Massacre. After the Boston Tea Party, Britain passed the Intolerable Acts. Each event made colonists angrier and more sure that Britain would not listen. By 1775, many felt that petitions and boycotts had failed, so when British soldiers marched to Concord, the militia fought back.

plan.text: Between 1763 and 1775, each conflict made the next one worse, until colonists believed peaceful protest had failed.
Boycotts got the Stamp Act repealed, but Parliament passed new taxes and sent troops to Boston, where soldiers killed five people in 1770.
After the Boston Tea Party, Britain punished Massachusetts with the Intolerable Acts in 1774.
Because Britain answered every protest with harsher rules, colonists stopped asking for change and started defying Britain, which is what rebellion is.

sentenceStarters: Each event made things worse because ___.
shortAnswerQuestions.lookAt: the timeline, and Chapter 2, Section 3 of the reading (From Protest to Rebellion).

shortAnswerQuestions.question: Which group (enslaved people, Native nations, women or Loyalists) saw independence differently from the Patriots, and why?
shortAnswerQuestions.rubric: Strong response names one group, explains what that group wanted or feared, gives a specific example (such as Dunmore's promise or western land), and contrasts it with what Patriots meant by liberty.
shortAnswerQuestions.exemplar: Enslaved people saw independence very differently from white Patriots. Patriots fought for liberty from British tyranny, but enslaved people had no liberty at all, and many of the people declaring independence were their enslavers. In 1775, Lord Dunmore promised freedom to enslaved people who escaped and joined the British, and thousands did. For them, the side that offered freedom mattered more than who ruled the colonies. The Patriots' talk of liberty did not include them.

plan.text: Enslaved people saw independence differently because the Patriots' liberty did not include them.
Many Patriot leaders, the people declaring independence, enslaved people themselves.
In 1775, Lord Dunmore promised freedom to enslaved people who joined the British, and thousands did.
For enslaved people, freedom from slavery mattered more than whether Britain or the Patriots ruled, so the British side could look like the side of liberty.

sentenceStarters: While Patriots wanted ___, this group wanted ___.
shortAnswerQuestions.lookAt: Chapter 2, Sections 1 and 2 of the reading (Three Choices; Choosing for Freedom and for Land).

shortAnswerQuestions.question: Whose rights did "all men are created equal" protect in 1776, and whose did it leave out?
shortAnswerQuestions.rubric: Strong response says whose rights were protected (mostly white men who owned property), names at least two groups left out with a specific example for each, and explains the contradiction between the words and the reality.
shortAnswerQuestions.exemplar: In 1776, the Declaration's rights mostly protected white men who owned property. They could vote and take part in the new government. Enslaved people were left out completely: they had no liberty, and Jefferson, who wrote "all men are created equal," enslaved people himself. Women almost everywhere could not vote or hold office. The Declaration even calls Native people "merciless Indian Savages." This shows the Declaration's promise of unalienable rights was not yet true for most people in America.

plan.text: In 1776, the Declaration's rights mostly protected white men who owned property and left most other people out.
Enslaved people had no liberty at all, and the author of "all men are created equal," Thomas Jefferson, enslaved people himself.
Women almost everywhere could not vote or hold office, and the Declaration calls Native people "merciless Indian Savages."
This shows a contradiction: the Declaration promised unalienable rights to everyone but protected them for only some.

sentenceStarters: In 1776, the Declaration protected the rights of ___.
shortAnswerQuestions.lookAt: Chapter 3, Section 3 of the reading (Grievances, and Who Was Left Out).

shortAnswerQuestions.question: When did the colonists' protest become rebellion, and what made that moment different from the protests before it?
shortAnswerQuestions.lookAt: Chapter 2, Section 3 of the reading (From Protest to Rebellion), and the timeline from 1773 to 1775.
shortAnswerQuestions.rubric: Strong response names one specific moment, explains the difference between asking a government to change and refusing to obey it, and uses a detail from before and after that moment.
shortAnswerQuestions.exemplar: I think protest became rebellion at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775. Before that, colonists protested by boycotting British goods and sending petitions, which asked Britain to change its laws. At Lexington, minutemen stood against British soldiers with guns, and at Concord they chased the army back to Boston. That was different because they were no longer asking Britain to listen; they were refusing to obey it.

plan.text: Protest became rebellion at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775.
Before 1775, colonists boycotted British goods and sent petitions asking Britain to change its laws.
At Lexington and Concord, minutemen fought British soldiers and chased them back to Boston.
Protest asks a government to change; rebellion refuses to obey it, and fighting the king's army is refusing to obey.

sentenceStarters: I think protest became rebellion when ___.

shortAnswerQuestions.question: Why does the person you are researching for your podcast deserve a place in the story of the Revolution?
shortAnswerQuestions.lookAt: your research notes and sources, and Chapter 4, Section 1 of the reading (The Voices Left Out).
shortAnswerQuestions.rubric: Strong response makes an arguable claim about the person's significance (a thesis, not a fact), supports it with at least two specific facts from credible sources, and explains why the usual story leaves the person out.
shortAnswerQuestions.exemplar: James Armistead Lafayette deserves a place in the story because his spying helped win the war's last major battle, yet the country he helped free did not free him. In 1781 he posed as a runaway helping the British while reporting their plans to the Marquis de Lafayette, and his reports helped trap the British at Yorktown. After the war, he had to petition the Virginia legislature for his own freedom. His story shows that the Revolution was won by people whose liberty it did not promise.

plan.text: James Armistead Lafayette deserves a place in the story because his spying helped win at Yorktown, yet he was not free.
In 1781 he posed as a runaway helping the British while reporting their plans to Lafayette.
After the war, he had to petition the Virginia legislature for his own freedom.
His story shows the Revolution depended on people whose liberty it did not promise, which is why the usual story leaves him out.

typingPassages.title: A Costly Victory, a Growing Anger
typingPassages.passage: In 1763, Britain won the French and Indian War, but winning nearly doubled its debt. To avoid a new war with Native nations, the king issued the Proclamation of 1763, a British order banning colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains. Colonists who had fought for that land were furious. Then Parliament passed new taxes, like the Stamp Act of 1765, to help pay for the war. The colonists had no members in Parliament, so they called this taxation without representation: being taxed by a government in which you have no elected voice. They fought back with a boycott, an organized refusal to buy certain goods as a form of protest. British merchants lost money, and in 1766 Parliament voted to repeal the Stamp Act, which means to officially cancel a law. The calm did not last. After the Boston Tea Party in 1773, Parliament passed the Intolerable Acts, laws punishing Massachusetts that closed the port of Boston and took away much of the colony's self-government. Britain hoped to frighten the other colonies. Instead, they sent food to Boston and met together at the First Continental Congress.

typingPassages.title: Patriot, Loyalist, or Neither
typingPassages.passage: As protest turned into war, every colonist faced a choice. A Patriot was a colonist who supported independence from Britain. Patriots led boycotts, joined the Sons and Daughters of Liberty, and later fought in the Continental Army. A Loyalist was a colonist who stayed loyal to Britain and the king during the Revolution. Historians estimate that about one in five white colonists were Loyalists. Many other people tried to stay neutral, choosing not to take either side in a conflict. Enslaved people and Native nations weighed the choice differently. In 1775, Lord Dunmore promised freedom to enslaved people who escaped and fought for Britain, and thousands did. Most Native nations sided with Britain, hoping to protect their land from settlers. On April 19, 1775, fighting began at Lexington and Concord. Protest had become rebellion, which is open, organized resistance against a government or authority. Protest asks a government to change. Rebellion refuses to obey it. When the king rejected a final peace offer and declared the colonies in rebellion, many undecided colonists began to think about breaking away for good.

typingPassages.title: The Words of 1776
typingPassages.source: Written for the Revolution unit, quoting the Declaration of Independence
typingPassages.passage: On July 4, 1776, Congress approved the Declaration of Independence. Independence means freedom from control by another country, and the right of a people to govern themselves. Thomas Jefferson wrote that all men are created equal and are born with unalienable rights, rights that belong to every person and cannot be taken away or given up. Among these rights are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. The Declaration also said that governments get their just powers from the consent of the governed, the idea that a government's power comes from the agreement of the people it rules. When a government destroys the rights it was created to protect, the people have the right to change it. Most of the Declaration is a list of grievances meant to prove that King George III was guilty of tyranny, the cruel and unjust use of power by a ruler or government. Yet the promise of equality had limits. About one in five people in the new nation was enslaved, women almost everywhere could not vote, and Native nations were described as enemies. Later Americans would use the Declaration's own words to demand the rights it had left out.

typingPassages.title: Recovering a Voice
typingPassages.passage: The usual story of the Revolution names only a few famous men, but the war depended on many more people. Overlooked voices are people whose real roles in history rarely make it into the usual telling of the story. James Armistead Lafayette, an enslaved man from Virginia, spied on the British in 1781, and his reports helped win the Battle of Yorktown. Deborah Sampson disguised herself as a man named Robert Shurtliff so she could fight. To tell their stories well, a historian needs strong sources. Credibility is how trustworthy and reliable a source of information is. Ask who made a source, when it was made, and why it was made, and check important facts in a second source. Next, build a thesis, a clear, arguable claim that your evidence works to prove. A thesis is not a topic and not a plain fact. It is a claim that someone could argue with. Finally, give credit with a citation, a note giving credit to the source your information came from. Citations let your listeners check your facts and show respect for the people whose work you used.

funFacts.text: The Stamp Act taxed almost every piece of printed paper in the colonies: newspapers, legal papers, diplomas, and even playing cards.
At the Boston Tea Party, colonists dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbor, about 92,000 pounds of it.
Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Native American descent, was one of the five people killed in the Boston Massacre. He is often called the first person to die in the American Revolution.
John Adams, a Patriot, was the lawyer who defended the British soldiers after the Boston Massacre. Most of them were found not guilty.
Congress voted for independence on July 2, 1776. John Adams predicted July 2 would be the day Americans celebrated forever.
Most delegates signed the official copy of the Declaration on August 2, 1776, not on July 4.
Thomas Jefferson was 33 years old when he wrote the first draft of the Declaration of Independence.
Common Sense sold tens of thousands of copies in its first few months, at a time when the colonies had about 2.5 million people.
Phillis Wheatley, kidnapped from West Africa as a child and enslaved in Boston, published a book of poems in 1773. It was the first book of poetry by an African American woman.
Deborah Sampson served in the Continental Army disguised as a man named Robert Shurtliff. After the war she gave paid talks about her service.
George Washington, writing in 1767, called the Proclamation Line "a temporary expedient," and kept claiming western land anyway.
The fight at Concord's North Bridge on April 19, 1775 is remembered as "the shot heard round the world," a line from an 1837 poem by Ralph Waldo Emerson.
